note.note:
History:
- 27-year-old male presents with 3 days of persistent, profuse watery diarrhea (nearly every hour while awake).
- Associated symptoms: crampy, mid-lower abdominal pain (intermittent, ~6/10), nausea, one episode of vomiting after having milk, self-reported subjective fever (“burning up”, no temperature measured).
- No blood in stools. No throat swelling or reported respiratory complaints.
- Reduced urinary frequency but still passing urine.
- Brother had similar symptoms for five days (now improving). No known food triggers or recent travel reported.
- Last attempted solid meal (lunch) passed as loose stool.
- No previous similar episodes reported.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic illnesses reported.
- No known drug allergies.
- Not on regular medications; has been using Paracetamol recently (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Family history: Father has stage 3 colon cancer.
- Social: Lives with mother and sister (not affected). Works in a government office.
- Lifestyle: Occasional social smoker; alcohol intake varies (heavier alcohol use 1-2 times/month).

Physical Examination:
- No physical exam findings documented (remote consult).
- Patient alert and able to converse throughout.
- No reports of confusion, severe lethargy, or inability to tolerate oral fluids.
- No mention of weight loss, rash, or joint pain.

Impression:
- Acute gastroenteritis, likely infectious etiology.

Management Plan:
- Advised to maintain hydration with clear fluids and oral rehydration solutions (e.g., Diarolyte—over-the-counter).
- Continue Paracetamol as needed for pain or fever (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Recommended soft diet (soup, mash) as tolerated; focus on hydration first.
- Advised to avoid alcohol.
- Close monitoring: to call back if symptoms persist >48 hours or if signs of dehydration worsen.
- No immediate investigations ordered in this consult.

Patient Summary:
- 27-year-old male with acute onset watery diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, and mild fever, consistent with presumed infectious gastroenteritis. No red flag symptoms or signs of severe dehydration at present. Supportive management and close outpatient monitoring have been advised.

Key Takeaways:
- Maintain oral hydration with clear fluids and oral rehydration solutions.
- Use Paracetamol as needed for pain or fever.
- Seek medical attention if symptoms do not improve in 48 hours or signs of dehydration develop.

Next Steps:
- Purchase oral rehydration solution (e.g., Diarolyte) from pharmacy.
- Monitor symptoms over next 48 hours; follow up with healthcare provider if no improvement or worsening occurs.
- No labs or referrals at present unless symptoms persist or worsen.
